Glassreach is thawing. Glass turns back into bark and leaf, and people step out of their own winters with their arms still raised, asking each other's names.

The Stilled wake over several weeks. Some are confused, some angry, some grateful. They need food, shelter and a way out. Yara's camp becomes a hall for them. A Stilled child asks for her mother, and somebody has to tell her.

Those who help the waking Stilled earn their trust. The thaw reaches the Glass Sexton last, if he is still in the glass.

playerWiki.title: Isolde's Demand
playerWiki.body:
Lady Isolde Drave follows you north. She arrives at the thaw with Hushmen, smiling. "What a lovely thaw. I'm told you have something of ours. The Frost Heart, let us say."

She offers a trade: give it to the Court and the Court will forget your interference. Refuse, and "the Court will remember it very precisely."

Isolde has silence-stone gloves, two Hushmen, and a very good memory. The Court has now followed you into the glass.

playerWiki.title: The Lightning Shafts
playerWiki.body:
The Lightning Shafts are old lightning-shafts that drop into the earth of Brassfall like the throats of bells. Thrane's bell hangs here. Storm-stones glitter pale blue and humming in the walls.

The sky above flickers, though there are no clouds. Somewhere below, a stone cracks like a whip. The Old Works lie close by, the abandoned mine where Old Garrow's ghost keeps watch.

A treasure room of storm-stones lies off the shafts. The stones discharge if picked up wrongly, and golems made of them guard the vault. Metal sparks near the stones.

playerWiki.title: Old Garrow
playerWiki.body:
Old Garrow is the ghost-foreman of the Old Works in Brassfall. He is gray-bearded, gruff and impatient, and he carries a lamp that burns blue. He calls everyone "lads and lasses." He died in a collapse years ago.

He asks the party to carry his lamp to his daughter, **Yenna**, in the Ironhorn foothills, near the camp, with a red horse-skull on her tent. Tell her he is sorry about the collapse, and tell her he is proud of her. "And don't drop it. It's the only thing down here that hums on purpose."

The lamp holds a storm-stone. He likes people who work hard and speak plainly.

playerWiki.title: The Sleeping Hall and the Sleepless
playerWiki.body:
The Sleeping Hall on Vael Tor is a cathedral of beds. Hundreds stand in rows climbing toward a ceiling of gray glass, and every one holds a sleeper who does not stir. Above the central bed hangs a bell the colour of old honey, its Heart missing. The air around it is very still.

At night the **Sleepless** come out. They take shapes drawn from the fears of the nearest sleeper. Anyone who rests on the Tor risks a nightmare, and a bad one can leave a Sleepless standing nearby in the morning.

The Hall belongs to Mirel's bell.

playerWiki.title: The Ironhorn Camp and the Heart-Hall
playerWiki.body:
The Ironhorn camp is a ring of white-hide tents with horse-skulls on their poles. Drums beat slow and steady. Riders cross the camp at a gallop, shouting names you do not know. The air smells of smoke, horse-sweat and something sharp like lightning.

At the centre stands the **Heart-Hall**, a long hall of white hide. A bronze clapper hangs there from a horse-skull and hums. It is Thrane's Heart.

Guests are welcome, and a guest wins a wager or buys dinner. The Thane's Ring is where the clans meet to decide things.

playerWiki.title: Thane Oru Kessa
playerWiki.body:
Thane Oru Kessa leads the Ironhorn Compact and holds Thrane's Heart. He is huge and bearded, with braids of bronze wire and a weathered, open face. He is blunt and funny and enjoys a wager. He calls everyone "rider," whatever their skill.

He welcomes the party as guests and sets a steppe contest. Win, and he opens the Heart-Hall. Lose, and "you'll leave me something to melt."

In private he says he is dying. Thrane's Heart has been eating his hands since he took it from the Brass Road. He hopes the Court's Key can cure lightning-sickness, and he wants to ring Thrane and bring the storms back. He asks an oath that the Heart be returned to his hall afterwards.

playerWiki.title: Yenna Garrow
playerWiki.body:
Yenna Garrow is a rider of the Ironhorn Compact, Old Garrow's daughter. She keeps the horses at the foothills camp. She is sun-darkened, with a red horse-skull on her tent and a long bronze braid she has never cut.

She is quiet and gruff like her father, but quicker to smile. She respects anyone who carries a debt honestly.

If you bring her the lamp, she weeps and thanks you. If you tell her what her father said, she gives something in return: a horse, a bow, or a bargain with her clan. She wants her father to rest.

playerWiki.title: The Hush Cult
playerWiki.body:
Robed figures sit in a circle around a dying fire on Vael Tor, humming very softly. When they see you, they smile, and the smile is sad and kind and terribly tired. "Rest, friends. You're so tired. Why not rest here, where the song is kind?"

The Hush Cult offers rest, dreamless sleep and an end to the Sleepless, in exchange for one night by the Hush Shrine. They speak in soft, persuasive voices and they want the world kept quiet forever.

They defend the shrine if attacked. They are not hostile unless pushed.

playerWiki.title: Corin Aldeth
playerWiki.body:
Corin Aldeth is a Bellwright. He is thin, with burn-scarred hands and a leather apron, and he listens with one ear turned. He hums under his breath. He is passionate, sharp and occasionally poetic.

His hidden workshop lies beneath a Brassfall tavern, full of bells in various stages of repair. "My family has tried to finish a song for three generations, and I think you may be the first people in a century who can help me finish it."

He wants to ring the Seventh Bell, and he shows the party Edda Thorne's Notes. He says the Seventh asks its Ringer for all six Tolls. He is enthusiastic about anyone who has rung one.

playerWiki.title: Edda Thorne's Notes
playerWiki.body:
Edda Thorne's Notes are the Bellwrights' copy of the tuning pages from Edda's diary. The diary itself lies in the Court's vault.

Corin shows you the Notes in his workshop. He says they describe a safe way to ring the Seventh Bell. He admits the price is high: the Seventh asks its Ringer for all six Tolls, and everyone else risks the world they know.

He gives you the Notes if you agree to help him. The pages also tell the story of the Quiet Night in Edda's own words.

playerWiki.title: The Hush Shrine
playerWiki.body:
Stairs spiral down into the hill under Vael Tor, each step worn smooth by feet that came to listen. Your footsteps are muffled, though the stone is bare. Far below, in darkness, a great bell hangs, its surface blank as a sleeping face.

You can walk a few steps down and hear the Hush. It speaks in the voice of your own sleeping self: "Be quiet now. You're so close. I've held everything together for four hundred years, and I'm so tired. If you wake me, the dream will end."

Corin Aldeth comes up the stairs. "Mirel first. Ring her wrong, and the Hush will sing you to sleep before the Court can arrest you. Let me help you do it right."

playerWiki.title: Thrane Rings
playerWiki.body:
Thrane cracks like a whip. The sky above Brassfall splits open, and for the first time in four centuries a real storm rolls over the mountains. Rain falls like bronze filings. Lightning strikes the peaks in long white bars. The storm-stones blaze, and every metal object you carry hums in answer.

The Ironhorn celebrate in the rain. The mines become dangerous, but the ore can be recovered.

The Ringer paid Thrane's Toll: a sense. The Court will hear of it.

playerWiki.title: Mirel Rings
playerWiki.body:
Mirel rings in the Sleeping Hall like a lullaby sung by someone who loves you. Every sleeper on the Tor sighs and turns over. The Sleepless dissolve into mist. For a moment the air feels like the first morning of spring, and you feel, impossibly, hopeful.

The Sleepless stop walking. The Hush's lullaby changes key, and it sounds sad, then grateful. The Cult weeps.

The Ringer paid Mirel's Toll: a fear the bell gave them. Hushmen are reported on the road, sent to the Tor to investigate.

playerWiki.title: What the Key Is
playerWiki.body:
Edda Thorne's tuning pages, read at last, tell the story of the Quiet Night in her own words. Imber wanted to tune the seven into one long spring. Edda told him the Seventh is not a bell but the lullaby. The Key is not a tuning tool. It is the heart that sings the Dreamer to sleep.

You now understand: the Seventh bell keeps **Oum**, the Dreamer, asleep. The Key is the Seventh's Heart, and the only Heart that can ring it. Imber struck the Key against the bells on the Quiet Night, and the discord cracked the lullaby. The bells went silent because the dream was waking.

Maudrin has known this since she took the Key. She kept it from the Court and the Church. Now she is marching, with the Key in a silence-stone case on a chain around her neck.

playerWiki.title: The Stormwall Loosens
playerWiki.body:
Since the storm broke over Brassfall, news has come up from Pellmoor. Pilots say the Seam has widened. Ships report calmer water at the edge of the Stormwall, and sails that were not there last month.

Nobody can say why. The timing is hard to ignore.

More ships than usual are arriving at Pellmoor.

playerWiki.title: The Strike
playerWiki.body:
Hushmen on grey horses come over the ridge in a long line. Their gloves catch the light and throw it back as silence. Behind them rides a figure in dove-grey, white-haired, with a face you have seen in your dreams.

"Good evening," Maudrin Vesk says, her voice carrying perfectly over the wind. "I'm so sorry to interrupt. But I believe you have something that belongs to me."

She wants the Hearts you carry, and the Key if you hold it. She offers a bargain: surrender them and be spared, or fight. Knights ride with her.

Beyond the ridge lies the foot of Vael Tor, where a ring of grey stones glows the colour of a dream you have almost forgotten.

playerWiki.title: The Summit of Vael Tor
playerWiki.body:
The stones of the Tor stand in a ring. In the centre, Maudrin Vesk waits with her Hushmen in a silent line. Behind her, the ground opens onto a spiral of stairs. The Hush rises from below like a tide, a lullaby so vast and low you feel it in your ribs.

"I'm glad you came," Maudrin says. "Shall we begin?"

She says she is the last person in Corvane who understands what the silence costs: four centuries of Tithes, Blanks, and children who forget their mothers. She asks whether you want to wake what holds it all together.

playerWiki.title: The Stairs of the Hush
playerWiki.body:
The stairs go on for a long time. Each step has a memory carved into it, worn smooth by the feet of those who came to listen. Some are your memories. Some are strangers'. You hear a child laughing, a bell tolling, a man telling a joke to someone who isn't there.

Every twenty steps costs a memory. The price is told at the first step, and anyone may turn back. Everyone who descends pays, allies included. 

The losses take recollections. They do not take skills, abilities or your own choices. At the bottom, a great bell hangs in darkness.

playerWiki.title: Ysh, the Seventh Bell
playerWiki.body:
Ysh, the Seventh Bell, hangs at the foot of the Stairs of the Hush. It is vast and blank, its surface like the face of a sleeping god. The lullaby is still there, very faint, asking you to be quiet.

Only the Key can strike it. Whoever rings it pays all six Tolls, Maudrin included. The Key is the Seventh's Heart, and the choice about what to do with it is the last one left in Corvane.

Everyone who comes down the stairs knows what is at stake.

pages.title: What’s It About?
pages.summary: Start here: the short pitch, session zero and your character.
pages.body:
What's It About?

Start here: the short pitch, session zero and your character. A player handout, no spoilers.

  • Setting: Corvane, in the Forgotten Realms
  • Rules: D&D 2024
  • Party: four characters, starting at level 3

The four handouts

  1. What’s It About? (this page). Start here: the short pitch, session zero and your character.
  2. The Seventh Bell. How the campaign works: the bells, their Hearts, the Toll, magic and who’s who.
  3. The Ringing Land. The world: Pellmoor Landing, the ships, and memory as money.
  4. The Map of Corvane. Where everything is, and how many days it takes to get there.

The short version

Four hundred and twelve years ago, every bell in Corvane fell silent in a single night. The dawn went grey. Winter froze into glass. The dead stopped resting. People learned to live without bells, and they paid for their forgetting in memories.

Thirty years ago, ships from the Sword Coast found a way through the storm that had hidden Corvane for centuries. They land at Pellmoor Landing, a busy port on a drowned lake.

Now something bronze is humming under that lake, and a fourteen-year-old girl can hear it. You are the people who find out why.

What you'll be doing

You'll be looking for the bells' Hearts: the bronze clappers that make each bell ring. Some are hidden. Some are guarded. Some are in the hands of people who want very different things from them.

Ringing a bell restores something that was lost. It also costs the person who rings it something of their own: the Toll. The DM always warns you before you ring: what kind of thing the bell will take, and how heavy it will be. Never exactly what. You can always walk away.

The question at the heart of the game: what do you want to ring, and what will it cost you? There is no single right answer.

Tone

ExpectHow muchWhat that means
MysteryA lotWhy did the bells stop? What is humming in the lake?
Hard choicesA lotEvery bell has a price, and there is no single right answer.
RoleplayPlentyTired, careful people who are sometimes kind when you least expect it.
ExplorationPlentyGlass forests, bronze mountains, a drowned lake, a sleeping hill.
CombatSomeIt happens, but it's rarely the only answer.
MoodMelancholy, not hopelessCold, mist and long quiet moments. Pellmoor is the loud exception.

Session zero

Before the first game we'll agree what the game should include and what it should leave out. Everyone gets a say, and you can answer in private.

WordWhat it meansExample
Off-limitsNever in the game, not even mentioned."Spiders are off-limits."
Off-screenCan happen in the story, but we skip past it without describing it."Torture stays off-screen."

Anyone can say "off-limits" or "off-screen" at any time, even mid-scene, and we change course without asking why. The campaign touches on drowning, harm to children, memory loss and family separation; say so if any of those should be off-limits or off-screen.

Your character

Any class, species and background from the 2024 Player's Handbook works. You start at level 3 with your subclass chosen, as one of four characters. You can be a newcomer who just arrived by ship, a Faerûnian who settled in Pellmoor years ago, or someone born in Corvane (The Ringing Land has more on each).

Some ideas, if you want a starting point:

  • Bell-touched. You can hear one silent bell, and you can't stop hearing it.
  • Already paid. You've sold or given away a memory, and you know something is missing.
  • Ferry-hand or pilot. You know the Mere and the names it has taken.
  • Court clerk or Dawn knight. Orderly, sworn, and starting to have doubts.
  • Bellwright's apprentice. You learned a hunted craft.
  • Sailor or trader from the Sword Coast. Your ship sailed without you, or you came to buy memories.

Bring to session zero

  • A level 3 character, with your subclass chosen.
  • One reason your character is in Pellmoor.
  • Anything you want off-limits or off-screen (you can tell the DM privately).
  • Someone your character would pay to remember, or would forget on purpose.

Questions to think about. You don't have to share your answers.

  • What would your character give up to remember someone they lost?
  • Is there a person your character would forget on purpose?
  • What do you owe a stranger who is suffering?
  • When would your character break an oath?
  • Would your character ring a bell that might end the world, if it might also save one person?

pages.title: The Seventh Bell
pages.summary: How the campaign works: the bells, their Hearts, the Toll, magic and who’s who.
pages.body:
The Seventh Bell

How the campaign works: the bells, their Hearts, the Toll, magic, and who's who. A player handout, no spoilers.

  • Setting: Corvane, in the Forgotten Realms
  • Year: 412 since the Silence (1492 DR)
  • Rules: D&D 2024
  • Party: four characters, starting at level 3

The four handouts

  1. What’s It About?. Start here: the short pitch, session zero and your character.
  2. The Seventh Bell (this page). How the campaign works: the bells, their Hearts, the Toll, magic and who’s who.
  3. The Ringing Land. The world: Pellmoor Landing, the ships, and memory as money.
  4. The Map of Corvane. Where everything is, and how many days it takes to get there.

On this page

  1. The story
  2. The seven bells
  3. Hearts and the Toll
  4. Magic
  5. Who's who
  6. Where you'll go

The story

Corvane is a land far out in the Trackless Sea, hidden for centuries behind a wall of storm. Seven great bells once kept its world in shape: dawn, memory, winter, harvest, storm, dreams and sleep.

Four hundred and twelve years ago, every bell fell silent in a single night, the Quiet Night. The dawn went grey. Winter froze into glass. The dead stopped resting. People learned to live without bells, and they paid for their forgetting in memories.

Thirty years ago a way through the storm opened, and ships from the Sword Coast began to arrive at Pellmoor Landing, a port on a still, drowned lake called the Mute Mere.

Now something bronze is humming under that lake, and a fourteen-year-old girl can hear it. You are the people who find out why.

The seven bells

Each bell kept one part of life in its proper form. The days of the week are still named for them, though nobody alive has heard one ring.

BellWhat it keptSince the silenceIts day
VaerDawn, law and beginningsThe sky never fully brightens over the capital. Lamps burn in the streets all day.Vaerday: good for oaths and contracts
OssaMemory, ancestors and restThe dead cannot rest. Their memories bleed into still water.Ossday: people visit graves
HiemeWinter and enduranceWinter froze into glass in Glassreach, and hasn't moved since.Hiemeday: cold; shops close early
CallaHarvest and generosityHarvests fail. Farmland north of the capital has gone to ash.Calladay: market day
ThraneStorm and courageNo storm has reached Brassfall since the Quiet Night.Thranday: travel is thought unlucky
MirelDreams and hopeNightmares walk the roads.Mirelday: people share their dreams
YshSleep and peaceNobody you know can say where the seventh bell hangs.Hushday: nobody starts anything important

Hearts and the Toll

A bell rings only with its Heart: the heavy bronze clapper that swings inside it. Some bells still hang without theirs. The Hearts are scattered across Corvane: some hidden, some guarded, some in the hands of people who want very different things from them. You'll be looking for them.

Ringing a bell restores something that was lost. It also costs the person who rings it something of their own: the Toll.

How a ringing works

  1. You find a bell's Heart and bring it to its bell.
  2. The DM warns you: what kind of thing this bell takes, and how heavy it will be. Never exactly what.
  3. You choose. Ring and pay, or walk away and nothing is taken.
TollWhat it touches
A memorySomething you remember. You may still know it happened.
A yearYour years.
A senseSight, hearing, taste, smell or touch.
A nameSomeone's memory of you.
A fearWhat you are afraid of.
A giftSomething you value, given to someone in need.

Tolls last, and each bell you ring makes the next one cost more. A Toll can never be bought back. What a bell gives back lasts too. Some bells you'll want to ring; some you'll want to leave silent.

Magic

  • Your spells work as written. In Corvane every spell hums faintly as it's cast; locals call magic Tonework. It adds no new costs. Divine magic from the Faerûnian gods works here too.
  • Silence-stones stop magic. The Quiet Court uses grey silence-stones. Spells fail within about 10 feet of one. You always see the edge first: the light dims and your ears feel pressure.
  • Stones can be broken. A stone isn't a spell, so dispelling won't help. Smash it (AC 12, 10 hit points), carry it off, or step out of its range.
  • The gloves don't stop you. The Court's Hushmen wear silence-stone gloves that only muffle their own blows. You can cast right next to one.
  • Be discreet inland. In Pellmoor, cast as loudly as you like. Inland, Hushmen call loud magic “bell-work”, and open spellcasting in the capital draws attention like a drawn sword.

Who's who

GroupWho they areWhat they want
The Quiet CourtThe government, ruled from Hallowmere. Orderly, polite, and very good at making people forget.The bells never ringing again
The Dawn OrderHallowmere's own knights, sworn to Vaer by old tradition. They keep watch under a sky that never brightens.Oaths kept, and the dawn back
The BellwrightsA secret network of bell-makers, outlawed and hunted for three hundred years.The bells rung
The Drowned ChoirThe restless dead of the Mute Mere, singing their grief.To be remembered by name
The Ironhorn CompactHorse-clans of the northern steppe. Proud, blunt, wary of anyone after their bronze.Their bronze, and their freedom
The Ferry-folkThe old families of Pellmoor. They pilot every foreign ship across the drowned town and keep a ledger of every name the water has taken.Their dead remembered properly
The LandingMerchants and travellers from the Sword Coast who trade at Pellmoor.Profit, mostly in bottled memories

Where you'll go

The map handout shows where each place is and how many days it takes to get there.

PlaceWhat it is
Pellmoor LandingWhere the story begins. Corvane's only port for foreign ships, with the old ferry village at its edge.
The Mute MereA vast, perfectly still lake over a drowned town. Its water remembers the dead.
HallowmereThe grey capital on the Ninefold Shore. The Quiet Court and the Dawn Order.
Kell's CrossingA fork in the North Road. The farmland around it has gone to ash.
GlassreachA forest in the northwest where winter froze into glass. Bring a warm cloak.
BrassfallEastern mountains of bronze, full of old lightning that no longer strikes.
Vael TorA lone high hill with a hall full of sleepers. Dreams go there to walk.
The Ironhorn SteppeNorthern grasslands. Riders greet strangers with a wager.

What do you want to ring, and what will it cost you?

pages.title: The Ringing Land
pages.summary: The world: Pellmoor Landing, the ships, and memory as money.
pages.body:
The Ringing Land

The world guide: Corvane, Pellmoor Landing, and how memory works as money. A player handout, no spoilers.

  • Now: 412 SS (since the Silence) = 1492 DR
  • Rules: D&D 2024
  • The story begins in: Pellmoor Landing

The four handouts

  1. What’s It About?. Start here: the short pitch, session zero and your character.
  2. The Seventh Bell. How the campaign works: the bells, their Hearts, the Toll, magic and who’s who.
  3. The Ringing Land (this page). The world: Pellmoor Landing, the ships, and memory as money.
  4. The Map of Corvane. Where everything is, and how many days it takes to get there.

On this page

  1. Where Corvane is
  2. Thirty years of ships
  3. Pellmoor Landing
  4. Memory is money
  5. Three ways to arrive
  6. Words you'll hear

Where Corvane is

Corvane is a continent called Hesk, part of the Forgotten Realms, far out in the Trackless Sea past the edge of every Sword Coast chart.

A permanent band of storm circles it at sea, thirty to sixty miles deep. Sailors call it the Stormwall. For four hundred years no ship crossed it, and nobody on either side knows what made it. Sword Coast sailors only had stories of "the Ringing Land" beyond the storm.

There is one way through: the Seam, a lane of calm water a mile or two wide. It opens at the mouth of the river Pell, which runs inland to the Mute Mere and Pellmoor Landing.

The voyage: Sword Coast → about six weeks at sea → the Seam (about a day, with a pilot) → the river Pell (two days) → Pellmoor Landing.

Ships sail from spring to early autumn.

Thirty years of ships

What everyone in Pellmoor knows.

WhenWhat happened
0 SS
(about 1080 DR)		The Quiet Night. Every bell in Corvane falls silent at once.
382 SS
(1462 DR)		The Wrongweather. For one night a storm comes up the river onto the Mute Mere, the first weather the Mere has seen in nearly four hundred years. People drowned. At dawn a battered Baldur's Gate ship, the Gull's Wager, drifts onto the lake: the first Faerûnians in Corvane in four centuries.
384 SS
(1464 DR)		The Landing Charter. The Quiet Court makes Pellmoor the only harbour where foreign ships may anchor. Foreigners may trade there freely but need a Court writ of passage to travel inland.
412 SS
(1492 DR)		Now. Forty to sixty ships a season. The old ferry village has become a port of about four thousand people. In summer, nearly twice that many crowd the waterfront.

Pellmoor Landing

The Mute Mere is so still that the ships look painted on it. A drowned town lies just under the water, its rooftops like the backs of sleeping animals, so every ship needs a local pilot to reach the quays.

The four districts

DistrictWhat's there
The Old ShoreThe original ferry village: reed-roofed houses, the ferry-dock, a small chapel with a silent bell, the Inn of the Shuttered Bell, and the Memory Shore, where names are scratched on stones. The ferry-folk keep it theirs.
The QuaysPiers built over the drowned town, warehouses and a dry-dock. The Pilots' Hall, and the Landing House (the Court's customs office).
The TallyThe market square, where both kinds of money change hands. The Reckoning House posts the day's rate by its door.
Strangers' RowThe Faerûnian quarter: foreign inns (the Brass Lantern is the best known), merchant houses, a temple mission of Lathander, and a clockmaker who sells silent clocks.

People you might hear about

NameWho they are
Dorra PellKeeps the Inn of the Shuttered Bell. Doesn't like questions. Remembers every face.
Brannagh WickPilot-Mistress of the Pilots' Hall. No ship moves on the Mere without one of her pilots.
Sela MauntA licensed Reckoner at the Reckoning House. Patient with newcomers.
Orsolo VennA rich Amnian merchant, the biggest buyer of memories in Pellmoor. Calls everyone "friend."
Sister AurelieA priestess of Lathander who runs the mission on Strangers' Row.
Tobias QuillThe Landing House's Tithe officer. Polite, grey-gloved, always carrying a form.

Rules of the Landing

  • Foreigners pay a 5 gp landing fee and register at the Landing House.
  • Without a writ of passage, a foreigner may go no further than the Mere road.
  • Clocks must be silent. The Landing House removes every chime.
  • The Court's grey-gloved officers, the Hushmen, walk the Old Shore every week.
  • There are no gulls on the Mere, and ferry-folk children don't play near the water.

Memory is money

In Corvane a memory can be taken out of you, sealed in a small glass vial, and spent. Gold arrived with the ships thirty years ago, and in Pellmoor most stalls take either.

How it works

  1. Drawing. A licensed Reckoner draws the memory out with a tuning fork. It takes about a minute and only ever happens with your consent.
  2. Sealing. The sealed vial is called a keep. It glows faintly and hums when you hold it. Nobody knows what's inside unless it's opened.
  3. Spending. Keeps are passed from hand to hand, still sealed, like banknotes.
  4. Opening. If you open your own keep, the memory comes back to you. If someone else opens it, they live the memory as a guest, without becoming you. It fades each time; after three strangers have opened it, it is spent.

What memories are worth

KindWhat it holdsIn PellmoorIn the capital
MoteA passing memory: last week's supper, a stranger's coatabout 1 spabout 8 cp
KeepA memory with feeling: a good afternoon, a small winabout 1 gp 2 spabout 8 sp
HeartkeepA defining memory: a parent's face, a wedding day25–100 gp20–80 gp
KnowingA memory that holds knowledge: a route, a recipe, a password. Whoever sells it forgets it.depends on usedepends on use

Good to know

  • Some things can't be sold: skills, spells, languages, anything you can do. "You can sell the day you learned to swim, but never the swimming."
  • The Tithe. The Quiet Court takes its tax in memories and says it protects people in return. A Tithed memory goes into a jar in the Court's vaults. People who give away too much stop recognising their own families; they're called Blanks.
  • Gold and the Court. Corvanese must pay their Court taxes in memory; foreigners pay in gold. Paying someone's tax for them in gold is called gilding. It's illegal, and it happens every day.
  • The capital's gate. Hallowmere asks every visitor for a small "courtesy memory" at the gate, and won't take gold instead.

At our table

  • You can pay with a memory anywhere coin is accepted in Corvane, at the posted rate. A Reckoner who buys a memory for gold keeps a tenth as a fee.
  • You always choose the memory. Write one line about it on your sheet, and tell the DM.
  • Motes and keeps change nothing on your character sheet.
  • If you sell a heartkeep, rewrite one thing it held up for your character: a belief, a bond, a fear.
  • Giving a memory freely to someone who needs it may earn Heroic Inspiration.
  • Ringing a bell costs a Toll, which is different: you are always warned first, and a Toll can never be bought back.

Three ways to arrive

Pick the one that suits your character. All three start in Pellmoor.

StormbornLanderBellfolk
WhoA Faerûnian who just arrived by ship, maybe this morningA Faerûnian who came years ago and stayedBorn in Corvane
You knowThe Sword Coast. Almost nothing about Corvane.Both worlds, a little. How to pay in memory.The Tithe, the Hushmen, the old customs
LanguagesCommonCommon, and Hesk if you've been here a yearHesk, and Common if you work the quays
Watch forYou need a writ to travel inland past the Mere roadNeither side thinks you quite belongForeigners treat your home as a curiosity
  • Species. Most Corvanese are human, with halfling ferry families and old dwarven mining clans. Elves are rare. Dragonborn, tieflings, orcs, goliaths, gnomes and aasimar came with the ships, and people stare (more curious than hostile).
  • Faith. Corvane's own church, the Ninefold Church, worships the Silence and calls the Faerûnian gods "the loud gods." Their priests work freely in Pellmoor. In the capital, the Court forbids foreign dawn-worship. Divine magic works normally.
  • Backgrounds. Any 2024 background works. Sailor, Merchant, Guide, Scribe, Sage, Acolyte, Wayfarer and Guard fit a port town naturally.

Some reasons to be in Pellmoor

  • Your ship sailed without you, and the next one is a month away.
  • You came to buy memories, or to sell yours.
  • You heard of a city where the sun never rises, and your god wants it to.
  • Someone you love sailed into the Stormwall and never came out.
  • You sold a memory years ago and you want it back.
  • You're ferry-folk, and a pilot you knew drowned six weeks ago.
  • You hear a hum at night that nobody else can hear.

Words you'll hear

Bellfolk
What Faerûnians call people born in Corvane.
Blank
Someone who has given away so many memories they no longer know their family.
Gilding
Paying a Corvanese person's tax in gold. Illegal.
Hesk
The land's own name for itself, and its language.
Hushman
An officer of the Quiet Court. Grey stone gloves. Very quiet.
Knowing
A sealed memory that holds knowledge. Whoever sells it forgets it.
Lander
A Faerûnian who has settled in Pellmoor.
Mote, keep, heartkeep
Sealed memories used as money, from least to most valuable.
Reckoner
The only person allowed to draw a memory out of someone.
The Seam
The one safe lane through the Stormwall.
SS
Years "since the Silence." 412 SS is 1492 DR.
Stormborn
The polite word for a Faerûnian. The rude one is "Loudfolk."
The Tithe
The Quiet Court's tax, paid in memories.
Tonework
What Corvanese call magic. Every spell hums as it's cast.
Writ of passage
The Court paper a foreigner needs to travel inland past the Mere road.

pages.title: The Map of Corvane
pages.summary: Where everything is, and how many days it takes to get there.
pages.body:
The Map of Corvane

Where everything is, and how long it takes to get there. A player handout, no spoilers.

  • Land: Hesk, in the Trackless Sea
  • Way in: the Seam, then the river Pell
  • The story begins in: Pellmoor Landing

The four handouts

  1. What’s It About?. Start here: the short pitch, session zero and your character.
  2. The Seventh Bell. How the campaign works: the bells, their Hearts, the Toll, magic and who’s who.
  3. The Ringing Land. The world: Pellmoor Landing, the ships, and memory as money.
  4. The Map of Corvane (this page). Where everything is, and how many days it takes to get there.

On this page

  1. The map
  2. Travel times
  3. The places

The map

Travel times

Roughly, on foot.

FromToTimeHow
The Sword CoastThe Seamabout 6 weeksBy sea, spring to early autumn
The SeamPellmoor Landingabout 3 daysA day through the Seam with a pilot, then two up the river Pell
PellmoorVael Tor3 daysThrough the Mere's eastern marsh
PellmoorKell's Crossing3 daysThe old Pellmoor track
PellmoorHallowmere6 daysVia Kell's Crossing; 3 by ferry across the Mere and then road
Kell's CrossingHallowmere3 daysThe North Road
Kell's CrossingGlassreach5 daysThe North Road through the Ninefold hills
Vael TorBrassfall4 daysThe Thrane Road
GlassreachBrassfall6 daysAround the Ironhorn foothills
BrassfallIronhorn Steppe2 daysUp into the foothills camps

Foreigners need a Court writ of passage to travel inland past the Mere road.

The places

Your characters know this much and no more.

Pellmoor Landing

Where the story begins. Corvane's only harbour for foreign ships: a busy port of quays, warehouses and foreign inns on the Mute Mere, with the old reed-roofed ferry village still standing at its edge.

Sounds like: a dozen languages arguing on the quays, and a hum under the water that some people pretend not to hear.

The Mute Mere

A vast, perfectly still lake with a drowned town beneath it. Its water remembers the dead. Spend a night on its shore and you may wake with a memory that was never yours.

Sounds like: nothing at all. Not even waves.

Hallowmere

The grey capital, on the Ninefold Shore. Terraces, archives and shuttered windows. Home of the Quiet Court and the Dawn Order.

Sounds like: footsteps, whispered business, and church bells that ring false.

Kell's Crossing

A fork in the North Road, where the old Pellmoor track comes in. The farmland around it has gone to ash.

Sounds like: wind over the fields, and a harvest-song nobody is allowed to sing.

Glassreach

A forest in the northwest where winter froze into glass. The people inside are still waiting for spring. Bring a warm cloak.

Sounds like: glass branches chiming against each other.

Brassfall

Eastern mountains of bronze, full of old lightning that no longer strikes. Miners pick their stones very carefully.

Sounds like: picks on bronze, and a crackle before a storm that never comes.

Vael Tor

A lone high hill in the middle of the land, with a hall full of sleepers. Dreams go there to walk.

Sounds like: breathing. Too many people breathing, slowly, all at once.

The Ironhorn Steppe

Northern grasslands held by the horse-clans of the Ironhorn Compact. Riders greet strangers with a wager.

Sounds like: hooves, laughter, and someone asking what you'll bet.

The Stormwall and the Seam

A ring of storm, thirty to sixty miles deep, circles the whole land at sea. For four hundred years nothing crossed it. Thirty years ago a calm lane opened at the mouth of the river Pell: the Seam. It drifts with the seasons, so every ship takes a pilot.

Sounds like: thunder that never stops, a long way off.

replace: A **Line** is something we never include. A **Veil** is something we can include, but we skip past it without describing it.
An **Off-limits** topic is something we never include. An **Off-screen** topic is something we can include, but we skip past it without describing it.
terms.note: The bells’ clappers are now called Hearts (Ossa’s Heart, Heart-Hound, Kessa’s Heart-Hall). The Tongues spell, “tip of your tongue” and Pellmoor’s “second tongue” are left alone. The session-zero safety words become Off-limits and Off-screen.
